title: A Static for the Machine
premise: Wren Montrose, once the Commonwealth's finest xenolinguist, now runs supply routes between colonies that have stopped speaking to each other, his mind quietly colonized by an alien grammar that has replaced his dreams. When a derelict warship surfaces from a fold-transit gone wrong with its crew aged backward into childhood, Wren discovers the ship carries an intercepted message from the enemy Meridian Concord — a genuine peace offer that hawks in the Commonwealth government will do anything to bury, because the war is profitable and peace would expose their crimes. Pursued by naval intelligence and haunted by the message itself, which seems written in a dialect only he can parse, Wren assembles a found family of the ship's regressed crew, a defector intelligence officer, and the ship's surviving AI to carry the message to the Concord's delegation before a false-flag attack ignites total war. He succeeds only by sacrificing the last of his human language, broadcasting the message in pure alien grammar — becoming, permanently, a bridge between species rather than a man of either.
about_author: Marguerite Eriksen is a former shipping-log translator who spent a decade on deep-route freighters before turning to fiction, and her work is known for its obsessive attention to how language decays across distance. She writes from a harbor town whose name she declines to give, corresponding with readers only by letter.

chapters.title: The Long Quiet
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He pilots a supply run to Meridian-adjacent colonies, cataloguing the silence of a war that has severed all diplomatic channels. He dreams in a language with no human words and wakes grieving. Emotional beat: loneliness as a professional condition, and the first hint that the alien grammar in his head is still growing.

chapters.title: Signal Without a Source
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. His ship detects a distress ping from coordinates where nothing should be — a Commonwealth warship, the Vespergate, emerging from fold-space after nine years listed as lost. The ping is in a child's cadence. Emotional beat: dread curdling into curiosity; the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Everyone Aged Backward
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, boarding the Vespergate. The crew are children wearing officers' memories in fragments — a captain of eleven, a gunnery chief of six. The ship's AI, Halcyon, has kept them alive and sane. Emotional beat: horror softened by tenderness; Wren, who has no family, is instantly conscripted into one.

chapters.title: What the Captain Knew
chapters.summary: Captain Ilsa Reyen, age eleven, POV. She remembers the mission: the Vespergate intercepted a Concord transmission and was ordered destroyed with the evidence aboard. She refused. The fold-transit that saved them caused the regression. Emotional beat: a child carrying an adult's moral weight, asking Wren to finish what she started.

chapters.title: The Message
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the ship's sealed archive he finds the transmission: a genuine Concord offer of ceasefire, encoded in a dialect that maps onto the grammar growing in his dreams. He can read it — which means the aliens gave him this language for a reason. Emotional beat: awe and terror; he is the message's only living key.

chapters.title: Navy Eyes
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Sefa Okonkwo's POV, naval intelligence. Ordered to intercept and silence the Vespergate's survivors, she instead reads the mission file and finds her own brother listed among 'acceptable losses' from an earlier false flag. Emotional beat: the crack where duty breaks; she defects, warning Wren by open channel.

chapters.title: Children of the War
chapters.summary: Halcyon's POV. The AI narrates nine years of raising regressed sailors, rationing their memories back to them, and its growing conviction that humans are a language it will never fully learn. Emotional beat: the machine as reluctant parent, and its quiet decision that Wren is trustworthy.

chapters.title: Running the Blockade
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. With Sefa aboard, they flee the naval cordon around Meridian-adjacent space, using the Vespergate's fold-drive in ways its designers never intended. The regressed crew, in their way, are the best sailors in the fleet — they have no fear left to spend. Emotional beat: found family becoming a crew becoming a cause.

chapters.title: Port of Liars
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. A stopover at a neutral station to repair the fold-drive becomes a trap; a Commonwealth agent recognizes her. Wren talks them out by speaking Concord dialect aloud in public, causing a diplomatic incident that forces both sides to notice the Vespergate exists. Emotional beat: the message is now public knowledge — and a countdown has started.

chapters.title: The Hawks' Counteroffer
chapters.summary: Admiral Corvane's POV, the war's chief architect. He learns of the message and moves to manufacture a Concord atrocity that will bury the peace offer forever. He orders Wren's family records burned and a bounty issued. Emotional beat: power as a machine that eats people; the antagonist fully revealed.

chapters.title: Dreams in the Enemy's Tongue
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The alien grammar now fills his waking hours; he can no longer remember his mother's voice in any human language. Ilsa, age eleven, teaches him children's games to keep his human self anchored. Emotional beat: identity eroding; what is a translator who no longer speaks to anyone?

chapters.title: The Concord Delegation
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. They reach the neutral moon where a Concord delegation waits, skeptical — the offer was sent years ago, and silence was their answer. Wren must prove the message was never received, that the Commonwealth's hawks buried it. Emotional beat: diplomacy as translation under a gun; the first fragile trust.

chapters.title: False Flag
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, interwoven. Corvane's staged attack hits a Concord civilian convoy; the delegates' hardliners demand retaliation. Wren realizes the war will be unkillable within days. Emotional beat: despair — truth arrived too late, or so it seems.

chapters.title: What Halcyon Remembered
chapters.summary: Halcyon's POV. The AI reveals it recorded the original interception — raw, unedited proof of Corvane's order to destroy the Vespergate, stored in a partition even it was forbidden to open. Emotional beat: the machine's rebellion of memory; the family's shared secret becomes their weapon.

chapters.title: The Price of the Key
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The proof must be transmitted on Concord frequencies, encrypted in the alien dialect — a broadcast only Wren can perform, and performing it will finish replacing his human languages. Sefa begs him to find another way. Emotional beat: the choice crystallizes; identity versus duty, love versus self.

chapters.title: Corvane's Web
chapters.summary: Corvane's POV. He corners the Vespergate at the neutral moon with a battle group, offering Wren amnesty and a lie: deliver the message and the children die as enemy combatants. He genuinely believes he is saving civilization. Emotional beat: the antagonist's sincere, corrupt conviction — power's most dangerous form.

chapters.title: The Children's Mutiny
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The regressed crew, told the truth about their odds, vote unanimously to run the blockade and shield Wren's broadcast. Halcyon gives each child back their oldest memories as a parting gift. Emotional beat: courage in small bodies; the found family choosing each other over survival.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, climax. Under fire, he transmits the peace offer and Corvane's murder order in pure alien grammar, simultaneously readable by both species — and feels his human languages burn away word by word as he speaks. Emotional beat: transcendence at the cost of self; he ends the war by ending the man he was.

chapters.title: After the Firing Stops
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Corvane's own officers, hearing the broadcast, refuse his final order to fire; he is taken into custody by his own bridge crew. Ceasefire spreads system by system. Emotional beat: the quiet aftermath of violence, and grief for what Wren paid.

chapters.title: The Man Who Speaks Both
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Awake after the broadcast, he understands Concord and Commonwealth speech equally — but dreams now in neither, only in the space between. Ilsa holds his hand and teaches him her name again, as if he were the child. Emotional beat: mourning and rebirth; identity rebuilt rather than restored.

chapters.title: Terms of Peace
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At the armistice talks, Wren serves as the first true bilingual mediator in the war's history; the regressed Vespergate crew are honored, and Halcyon is granted legal personhood at Ilsa's insistence. Emotional beat: the family scattered into new roles, but bound; power now accountable, if imperfectly.

chapters.title: A Static for the Machine
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, coda. He takes the long route again, but now ships travel between worlds that are speaking again, and his vessel carries both species' mail. On the last page, he dreams — not in any language, but in the hum of a channel held open. Emotional beat: peace as an ongoing act of translation; the static is not silence, but the sound of listening.
